raw_text:
# 1-Week Deload Protocol
### Client Profile Recap
**Age:** 26 | **Level:** Advanced | **Context:** Post 4-week high-volume hypertrophy block (avg. 18 working sets/session, RPE 8.5 compounds) | **Equipment:** Full gym

---

## Deload Philosophy & Targets

The goal this week is **systemic recovery without detraining**. After four weeks at high mechanical tension and metabolic stress, the nervous system, connective tissue, and muscular tissue all carry accumulated fatigue that is masking true fitness. This deload does not mean doing nothing — it means doing just enough to maintain motor patterns, flush metabolic waste, and arrive at Week 6 feeling genuinely fresh and primed for the next block.

**Volume target:** Drop to approximately **40–50% of working sets** — roughly 7–9 working sets per session rather than 18.

**Intensity target:** Drop load to approximately **50–60% of recent working weights**, keeping RPE firmly at **5–6 on all compound lifts**. Nothing should feel hard. If it does, reduce the load further. There is no heroism in a deload week.

**Rep ranges:** Keep rep ranges identical to the preceding block so motor patterns remain grooved, but the reduced load means bar speed will be high and effort will feel almost trivially easy. That is correct. Embrace it.

**Rest periods:** Can be shortened slightly (60–90 seconds) since fatigue accumulation is not the goal, but do not rush to the point of cardiovascular stress.

---

## Session Structure Overview

The week mirrors the training split from the preceding block. If the client was running a 4-day upper/lower or push/pull/legs structure, the same days apply. Below, the programme is written as a **4-day full-gym deload** using the same exercise selection from the hypertrophy block, with Monday/Tuesday/Thursday/Friday as the default layout and Wednesday/Saturday/Sunday as full rest or light walking only. Adjust days to match the client's actual split if different.

---

## Day-by-Day Programme

---

### **Monday — Upper Body (Push Focus)**

*Preceding block context: Chest, shoulders, triceps — likely 18 sets including bench variations, overhead press, flyes, lateral raises, tricep isolation.*

**Warm-up:** 8–10 minutes of light cardio (rowing machine or incline treadmill walk), followed by 2 rounds of band pull-aparts (15 reps), shoulder CARs, and thoracic rotations. Keep the warm-up purposeful but unhurried.

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Load | RPE Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Flat Bench Press | 3 × 8 | ~50–55% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Seated Dumbbell Overhead Press | 2 × 10 | ~50% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Incline Dumbbell Flye | 2 × 12 | Light — focus on stretch | 4–5 |
| Cable Lateral Raise | 2 × 15 | Very light | 4 |
| Tricep Rope Pushdown | 2 × 15 | Light | 4–5 |

**Total working sets: 11** *(down from ~18)*

**Session notes:** The bench press should feel almost embarrassingly light. That is the point. Use the reduced load to focus on technique — scapular retraction, leg drive, bar path. Treat every set as a technical rehearsal for the heavier loads coming in Week 6. Do not add sets. Do not add load. Log the session and leave.

---

### **Tuesday — Lower Body (Quad Focus)**

*Preceding block context: Squats, leg press, lunges, leg extension, possibly Romanian deadlift — high volume, high fatigue accumulation in quads and glutes.*

**Warm-up:** 8 minutes assault bike at easy pace, followed by 2 rounds of bodyweight squats (10 reps), hip flexor stretch (30 seconds each side), and glute bridges (12 reps).

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Load | RPE Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Back Squat | 3 × 6 | ~50% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Leg Press | 2 × 10 | ~50% of recent working weight | 4–5 |
| Walking Dumbbell Lunge | 2 × 10 each leg | Light dumbbells | 4–5 |
| Leg Extension | 2 × 15 | Light | 4 |

**Total working sets: 9** *(down from ~18)*

**Session notes:** The squat is the priority movement here. With the load reduced, the client should focus on depth consistency, bracing mechanics, and a controlled eccentric. Six reps per set is intentional — enough to groove the pattern without accumulating meaningful fatigue. The leg press and lunge serve as blood flow and pattern reinforcement, nothing more. Leg extension at the end is purely for quad pump and circulation.

---

### **Wednesday — Full Rest**

No structured training. Encourage a 20–30 minute easy walk outdoors if the client feels restless — this supports parasympathetic recovery and light circulation without adding training stress. No stretching sessions that push into discomfort. No "active recovery" that creeps into actual training.

---

### **Thursday — Upper Body (Pull Focus)**

*Preceding block context: Deadlift or rack pull, barbell/dumbbell rows, pull-ups or lat pulldown, face pulls, bicep curls — high posterior chain and lat volume.*

**Warm-up:** 8 minutes light rowing, followed by 2 rounds of band face pulls (15 reps), dead hangs (20 seconds), and cat-cow (10 reps).

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Load | RPE Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Barbell Conventional Deadlift | 3 × 4 | ~50% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Barbell Bent-Over Row | 2 × 8 | ~50% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Lat Pulldown | 2 × 12 | Light | 4–5 |
| Seated Cable Row | 2 × 12 | Light | 4–5 |
| Dumbbell Bicep Curl | 2 × 15 | Light | 4 |

**Total working sets: 11** *(down from ~18)*

**Session notes:** The deadlift rep count drops to 4 per set deliberately. Deadlifts accumulate spinal and hip fatigue quickly, and even at 50% load, higher rep sets can generate more systemic stress than intended during a deload. Four crisp, technically sound reps per set is sufficient. The client should feel the hinge pattern, brace properly, and focus on a smooth bar path. Rows and pulldowns are about maintaining lat activation and scapular mechanics, not chasing a pump.

---

### **Friday — Lower Body (Posterior Chain Focus)**

*Preceding block context: Romanian deadlifts, hamstring curls, hip thrusts, calf raises — posterior chain emphasis.*

**Warm-up:** 8 minutes incline treadmill walk, followed by 2 rounds of glute bridges (12 reps), banded clamshells (15 each side), and standing hip flexor stretch (30 seconds each side).

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Load | RPE Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Romanian Deadlift | 3 × 8 | ~50% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Barbell Hip Thrust | 2 × 10 | ~50% of recent working weight | 5 |
| Lying Hamstring Curl | 2 × 12 | Light | 4–5 |
| Standing Calf Raise | 2 × 20 | Light | 4 |

**Total working sets: 9** *(down from ~18)*

**Session notes:** The Romanian deadlift at reduced load is an excellent opportunity to reinforce the hip hinge under minimal fatigue — slow the eccentric to 3 seconds and feel the hamstring stretch fully at the bottom. Hip thrusts should feel smooth and controlled, not explosive. Calf raises at the end are largely for circulation and can be done with a slow, deliberate tempo to maintain ankle mobility.

---

### **Saturday & Sunday — Full Rest**

Two consecutive rest days to close the week. Encourage the client to prioritise sleep (targeting 8–9 hours), manage stress, and avoid any spontaneous "extra" training. If the client is genuinely restless on Sunday, a 20-minute easy walk or 15 minutes of light mobility work is acceptable, but nothing that elevates heart rate meaningfully.

---

## Nutrition Guidance for the Deload Week

Since training volume and intensity are significantly reduced, total energy expenditure drops. The following adjustments are recommended:

**Calories:** Reduce total daily intake by approximately **10–15%** relative to the hypertrophy block. This is not a dramatic cut — it simply reflects the reduced training demand. Maintaining a large caloric surplus during a deload when output is low risks unnecessary fat accumulation without the training stimulus to direct nutrients toward muscle protein synthesis.

**Protein:** **Hold protein intake constant** at the client's current target (likely 2.0–2.2g per kg of bodyweight). Protein remains the priority nutrient for tissue repair and recovery, which is precisely what this week is designed to facilitate. Do not reduce protein to hit a lower calorie target — reduce carbohydrates and fats proportionally instead.

**Carbohydrates:** A modest reduction in carbohydrates is appropriate given the lower glycolytic demand of the sessions. However, do not drop carbohydrates aggressively. Glycogen replenishment supports recovery, and the client should arrive at Week 6 with full glycogen stores. Aim for roughly **3.5–4.5g per kg** of bodyweight in carbohydrates across the week.

**Hydration:** Encourage consistent hydration throughout the week — a minimum of 3 litres of water daily. Adequate hydration supports connective tissue recovery and nutrient transport.

**Alcohol:** Advise the client to minimise or eliminate alcohol this week. Alcohol impairs sleep quality, blunts protein synthesis, and undermines the recovery the deload is designed to produce. One social drink is unlikely to be catastrophic, but a heavy weekend will meaningfully compromise the week's purpose.

---

## Recovery Protocols

**Sleep:** This is the single most important recovery tool this week. Encourage the client to target **8–9 hours per night**, with a consistent sleep and wake time. If the client has been running a sleep deficit during the hypertrophy block — which is common at high training volumes — this week is the opportunity to repay it.

**Soft tissue work:** 10–15 minutes of foam rolling or a sports massage mid-week (Wednesday is ideal) targeting the quads, hamstrings, glutes, lats, and thoracic spine. This is not mandatory but is highly recommended for an advanced client coming off four weeks of high-volume work. Keep pressure moderate — aggressive deep tissue work can itself create soreness and is counterproductive during a deload.

**Mobility:** 10 minutes of light mobility work on rest days is encouraged — hip flexor stretches, thoracic rotations, and ankle mobility drills. Keep it gentle and restorative, not a workout in disguise.

**Stress management:** Remind the client that psychological stress and training stress share the same recovery resources. If work or life stress is elevated this week, lean even further into the conservative end of the deload — reduce RPE targets to 4 if needed and prioritise sleep above all else.

---

## Key Coaching Cues for the Week

> *"If it feels too easy, you're doing it right."*

The most common mistake advanced clients make during a deload is adding load or sets because the prescribed work feels insufficient. Reinforce clearly that the fatigue masking fitness from the previous four weeks will not be apparent until it dissipates — and it only dissipates if the client actually rests. The client will not detrain in one week. They will, however, arrive at Week 6 significantly stronger and more recovered if they trust the process.

Log every session. Note how the movement patterns feel, whether any joints or muscles feel particularly fatigued or tight, and how energy levels change across the week. This information is valuable for programming the next block.

---

## Week at a Glance

| Day | Session | Working Sets | RPE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monday | Upper Push | 11 | 4–5 |
| Tuesday | Lower Quad | 9 | 4–5 |
| Wednesday | Full Rest | — | — |
| Thursday | Upper Pull | 11 | 4–5 |
| Friday | Lower Posterior | 9 | 4–5 |
| Saturday | Full Rest | — | — |
| Sunday | Full Rest | — | — |

**Weekly working set total: 40** *(vs. approximately 72 in a standard hypertrophy week at 18 sets × 4 sessions)*

---

*Week 6 begins the new block. The client should feel noticeably fresher, more motivated, and stronger by Friday of this week. If they do not, consider extending the deload by 3–4 days before loading back up.*
